evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published surveys.

claim: The skills and knowledge that PhD students and postdocs acquire during their training are useful in a range of careers both inside and outside academia.
source: We hope PhD students and postdocs will be reassured to learn that the skills and knowledge they acquire during their training are useful in a range of careers both inside and outside acaemica.
evidence: This is inferred from the diversity of career outcomes observed in the study.

claim: Further changes to the career landscape in the life sciences are likely in future as a result of the long-term impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic.
source: Further changes to the career landscape in the life sciences are likely in future, not least as a result of the long-term impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic (Bodin, 2020).
evidence: This is a speculation about future trends supported by a citation.

claim: A career service was launched at EMBL in 2019 for all PhD students and postdocs.
source: At EMBL, a career service was launched in 2019 for all PhD students and postdocs
evidence: This is a statement about an institutional initiative.

claim: The EMBL career service built on a successful EC-funded pilot project that offered career support to 76 postdocs in the EMBL Interdisciplinary Postdoc Programme.
source: building on a successful EC-funded pilot project that offered career support to 76 postdocs in the EMBL Interdisciplinary Postdoc Programme
evidence: This is a statement about the history of the career service.

claim: The trend towards fewer first-author articles per researcher likely reflects a global trend towards articles with more authors and a greater focus on collaborative and/or interdisciplinary approaches to research.
source: The trend towards fewer first-author articles per researcher likely reflects a global trend towards articles with more authors and a greater focus on collaborative and/or interdisciplinary approaches to research.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed publication trends.

claim: Working on a project that involves multiple partners provides an early-career researcher with the opportunity to develop a range of skills, including teamwork, leadership and creativity.
source: Working on a project that involves multiple partners provides an early-career researcher with the opportunity to develop a range of skills, including teamwork, leadership and creativity.
evidence: This is a statement about the benefits of collaborative research based on general knowledge.

claim: Multi-partner interdisciplinary projects allow researchers to tackle challenging biological questions from new angles to advance in their field of research.
source: Such projects also allow researchers to tackle challenging biological questions from new angles to advance in their field of research, something viewed very positively by academic hiring committees (Hsu et al., 2021; Clement et al., 2020; Fernandes et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Multi-partner interdisciplinary projects can take longer to complete.
source: however, multi-partner interdisciplinary projects can also take longer to complete
evidence: This is a statement about a potential challenge of collaborative research based on general knowledge.

claim: Open science practices can make project contributions more transparent and available faster.
source: For example, open science practices – including author credit statements, FAIR data, and pre-printing – can make project contributions more transparent and available faster (Kaiser, 2017; McNutt et al., 2018; Wilkinson et al., 2016; Wolf et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The retrospective, observational design of the study limits the ability to disentangle causation from correlation.
source: The limitations of our study include that its retrospective, observational design limits our ability to disentangle causation from correlation.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a methodological limitation.

claim: The changes in career outcomes may be driven primarily by increased competition for PI roles.
source: The changes in career outcomes may be driven primarily by increased competition for PI roles
evidence: This is a speculation about the causes of observed trends.

claim: The changes in career outcomes could be influenced by a greater availability or awareness of other career options.
source: but they could also be influenced by a greater availability or awareness of other career options
evidence: This is a speculation about alternative explanations for observed trends.

claim: EMBL has held an annual career day highlighting career options outside academia since 2006.
source: EMBL has held an annual career day highlighting career options outside academia since 2006
evidence: This is a statement about an institutional initiative.

claim: Many EMBL alumni decide to pursue a career in the private sector, attracted by perceptions of higher pay, more stable contracts, and/or better work-life balance.
source: and many of our alumni decide to pursue a career in the private sector, attracted by perceptions of higher pay, more stable contracts, and/or better work-life balance
evidence: This is a speculation about motivations for career choices.

claim: The study plans to update observational data every four years.
source: We plan to update our observational data every four years
evidence: This is a statement about future plans for the study.

claim: The study plans to maintain data on the career paths of alumni for 24 years after they leave EMBL.
source: and to maintain data on the career paths of alumni for 24 years after they leave EMBL
evidence: This is a statement about future plans for the study.

claim: The study included individuals who graduated from the EMBL International PhD Programme between 1997 and 2020 (n=969).
source: The study includes individuals who graduated from the EMBL International PhD Programme between 1997 and 2020 (n=969)
evidence: This describes the PhD student sample in the Methods section.

claim: The study included individuals who left the EMBL postdoc programme between 1997 and 2020 after spending at least one year as an EMBL postdoctoral fellow (n=1315).
source: or who left the EMBL postdoc programme between 1997 and 2020 after spending at least one year as an EMBL postdoctoral fellow (n=1315)
evidence: This describes the postdoc sample in the Methods section.

claim: Where a PhD student remained at EMBL for a bridging or longer postdoc, they were included as PhD alumni only, with the postdoc position listed as a career outcome.
source: Each person is included only once in the study: where a PhD student remained at EMBL for a bridging or longer postdoc, they were included as PhD alumni only, with the postdoc position listed as a career outcome.
evidence: This describes a methodological decision to avoid double-counting.

claim: An individual was classified as having a 'detailed career path' if an online CV or biosketch was found that accounted for their time since EMBL excluding a maximum of two one-calendar-year career breaks.
source: An individual was classified as having a "detailed career path" if an online CV or biosketch was found that accounted for their time since EMBL excluding a maximum of two one-calendar-year career breaks (which may, for example, reflect undisclosed sabbaticals or parental leave).
evidence: This describes the criteria for classifying detailed career paths.

claim: Calendar years were used for all outcome data.
source: We use calendar years for all outcome data – for example, for an individual who left EMBL in 2012, the position one calendar year after EMBL would be the position held in 2013.
evidence: This describes a methodological choice in data analysis.

claim: A Cox proportional hazards regression model was fitted to the data to predict time-to-event probabilities for each type of career outcome.
source: A Cox proportional hazards regression model was fitted to the data in order to predict time-to-event probabilities for each type of career outcome based on different covariates including cohort, publication variables and gender.
evidence: This describes the statistical method used in the analysis.

claim: Multivariate Cox models were fitted using a ridge penalty with penalty parameter chosen by 10-fold cross-validation.
source: Multivariate Cox models were fitted using a ridge penalty with penalty parameter chosen by 10-fold cross-validation.
evidence: This describes the statistical methodology.

claim: Harrell's C-index was calculated for each fit in an outer cross-validation scheme for validation and analysis of different models, with 10-fold cross-validation.
source: Harrell's C-index was calculated for each fit in an outer cross-validation scheme for validation and analysis of different models, with 10-fold cross-validation.
evidence: This describes the model evaluation methodology.
